query: For magnetic high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could increase the coercive field? State one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to alter coercivity, the predicted outcome relative to a matched baseline, the conditions under which the effect should hold, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of grain-refining elements, such as boron or carbon, into the magnetic high-entropy alloy will increase the coercive field.
generation.material_initial_state: Magnetic high-entropy alloy with a coarse grain structure
generation.intervention: Addition of grain-refining elements (e.g., boron or carbon) to the alloy
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under conditions that allow for uniform distribution of the grain-refining elements, and the resulting microstructure has a refined grain size
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size and grain boundary density
generation.mechanism: The introduction of grain-refining elements reduces the grain size, increasing the grain boundary density, which in turn pins magnetic domain walls, increasing the coercive field
generation.predicted_outcome: The coercive field of the alloy with grain-refining elements will be higher than that of the baseline alloy without these elements
generation.baseline: Magnetic high-entropy alloy without grain-refining elements
generation.boundary: The effect of grain-refining elements on coercivity will be most pronounced in alloys with initial coarse grain structures
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount and type of grain-refining elements, as well as the processing conditions, may vary depending on the specific alloy composition and desired properties

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of magnetic high-entropy alloy samples: one with and one without the addition of grain-refining elements. Measure the coercive field of both sets using a standardized method (e.g., vibrating sample magnetometry).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coercive field of the alloy with grain-refining elements is not significantly higher than that of the baseline alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

In all our studied entropy-stabilized oxides, the exchange bias is significantly greater than what is observed in the Pt/Py/CoO/MgO heterostructure (Fig. 3a,b). Our measured values for the Pt/Py/CoO/MgO sample agree with published results,, in which it was concluded that the spins on the (001) interface of CoO are well compensated and thus result in a small exchange bias (~0.1 kOe), even at low temperatures. Since it is known that there is significant local structural and chemical disorder in entropy-stabilized oxides, it would be expected that the magnetic lattice becomes frustrated on a local scale. This could result in a significant increase in the exchange strength, as it has been observed that exchange bias is strongly influenced by the density of disordered magnetic moments at the FM/AFM interface,,. We also suspect that this is the cause of the anomalous shape in the hysteresis curves shown in Fig. 2.
